newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir rebels say inspired by Afghan uprising. [CORRECTED 11:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Kashmir rebels say inspired by Afghan uprising. [CORRECTED 11:20 GMT]

text.p: Kashmir separatists vowed on Sunday to draw inspiration from the military success of the Islamic militia in Afghanistan, raising the prospect of an upsurge of violence in the troubled Indian region.

"One inspiration we have got on Friday is that people who fight for their rights...are victorious and successful," said Qazi Abdullah, a leader of the All Parties Hurriyat Conference, which groups some 30 Kashmir separatist groups.

On Friday, Taleban militia overran the Afghan capital Kabul, where it set up a strict fundamentalist Moslem government after capturing the city against little resistance at the climax of a sweep through eastern Afghanistan.
More than 20,000 people have died in India's Jammu and Kashmir state since a separatist revolt erupted in 1990. The state is mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority province.
India accuses Pakistan, which rules over one third of the Kashmir region, of arming guerrillas who are fighting for either independence or merger with Islamic Pakistan.
Islamabad says it provides only diplomatic and moral support to the Moslem militants in Kashmir.
"When the Taleban succeeded we got another inspiration. Slow and steady wins the race," the Hurriyat's Abdullah said.
"People who have consistency in their own fight, who have a right and genuine cause -- time will bring them victory, come the right moment."
A senior Indian army official in the state's summer capital Srinagar said he believed the Taleban's success could stoke militancy in Kashmir.
"It will encourage fundamentalism, and the situation will get more complicated in Afghanistan," Lt-General J.S. Dhillon, commander of the 15th Army Corps, told a local newspaper.
"We have to be careful as Pakistan will send more and more mercenaries to Kashmir," he said.
Dozens of militants groups are fighting Indian rule in Jammu and Kashmir. Authorities say some of the better armed groups include Moslem fundamentalists from other countries.
On Saturday, a rightist political party in Pakistan-ruled Kashmir said the Taleban had closed two camps in eastern Afghanistan that trained Kashmiri militants.

On Monday, the state holds the fourth and last stage of local assembly elections which Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left government in New Delhi hopes will pave the way to the restoration of normalcy in the region.

Twenty-one people, mostly political activists, have been killed during the month-long campaign. Farooq Abdullah, the leader of the state's biggest party, the National Conference, has escaped two grenade attacks.

State television said about 20,000 (corrects from "200,000") paramilitary troopers were posted to guard Monday's polls in Doda, 250 km (150 miles) south of Srinagar. Many of Kashmir's separatist outfits have hideouts in the district's bleak and inhospitable terrain.
Authorities detained most of the Hurriyat's senior leaders, fearing their outspoken opposition to the elections might encourage Kashmiris to disrupt polling.
Poll officials estimated about 300,000 people were eligible to vote for 45 candidates in six assembly segments on Monday.
Polling in the rest of the state is over. Vote counting begins on Tuesday and will take three days, authorities said.
National Conference leader Farooq Abdullah was tipped to become the state's next chief minister.
